children: Bolstered by good all-round traction across retail, agriculture and MSME (RAM) sectors alongside corporate loan book, private sector lender Karur Vysya Bank has upped its credit growth guidance to 18–20 per cent for FY27.

We are adopting a calibrated approach to corporate lending, with an average ticket size of ₹45–50 crore, rather than pursuing large exposures aggressively, Ramesh Babu, MD and CEO, Karur Vysya Bank, told media persons in an interaction. Predictive analytics and other collection efforts have helped the bank keep a close eye on asset quality as it grows the loan book, he said.

The private sector lender recorded a robust net profit growth of 37.3 per cent y-o-y at ₹788 crore for the quarter ended September 2026 (Q2FY27). Net interest income increased by 18.7 per cent to ₹1,497 crore from ₹1,261 crore for the corresponding quarter of the previous year.

When asked about the widening gap between  advances and deposits, Babu said its liquidity position remained comfortable, with the average liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) at around 129 per cent during the quarter.

The bank is also exploring fundraising in international markets, including through dollar-denominated bonds. Babu said KVB was working with a few partners and had undertaken preliminary due diligence but was not pursuing the exercise aggressively. “We are on the job. Maybe in the next one month or so, we will try to conclude some deal if the pricing is favourable to us,” he said.

KVB also guided for a 4 per cent NIM in FY27 despite reporting margins above 4.2 per cent for two consecutive quarters, as the bank expects competitive pricing pressures and a moderation in benefits from loan repricing to weigh on yields.

The substantial inflow of foreign currency non-resident (bank) or FCNR(B) deposits across banks could intensify competition for lending opportunities over the next one or two quarters, prompting lenders to price loans more aggressively to deploy the funds, Babu said.

“When they have paid 6.5 per cent, they have to get something more than that,” Babu said, referring to the cost of mobilising FCNR(B) deposits.
“We may have to be ready for some sort of a pricing pressure, if at all. That is the reason we kept some sort of a cushion as far as the yield on advances is concerned,” he added.
The bank mobilised around ₹685 crore in FCNR(B) deposits during the quarter with no leverage provided against these deposits as the Bank does not have an overseas branch.
While personal loan demand has picked up during the festive season, Babu says recovery has been weaker than in previous years.

“My opinion is that people are lying low and are conservative in spending,” he said, attributing the trend to inflation, market conditions and other uncertainties. Consumers could be postponing discretionary and impulse purchases until conditions normalise, he added.
KVB is also taking a cautious approach to housing loans amid intense competition and pricing pressures.

When asked if the proposed Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) guidelines could significantly affect the bank’s bancassurance income, Babu said it makes up a small share and estimated a 60–70 per cent decline in commissions.

KVB plans to mitigate the impact by increasing insurance penetration among its customers from 1.6 per cent to around 3.9 per cent, he said. The strategy includes optimising its product mix, reaching underserved customer segments and using customer analytics to address regional disparities in penetration, he added.

title: Karur Vysya Bank eyes 18–20% credit growth in FY27 on all-round demand
